title: Cleaning the Old Masters
subtitle: Removing old varnish can reveal a painting's true colours, but how can anyone be sure what the artist intended?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few activities in the art world arouse stronger feelings than the cleaning of famous paintings. Over time, the varnish that painters and later restorers applied to protect their work turns yellow and then brown, and it collects dirt and smoke. Removing it can transform a picture, revealing colours that have not been seen for centuries and details that had disappeared into the gloom. But cleaning cannot be undone, and critics have repeatedly accused museums of stripping away not only dirt but part of the original work itself. The debate has rarely been calm, and it has never been fully resolved.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty lies in the nature of varnish itself and in its long history. Until the twentieth century, most varnishes were made from natural resins dissolved in oil or spirits. These gave paintings a pleasing gloss when first applied, but they reacted with light and air, gradually darkening and becoming brittle, so that within a few decades a fresh coat was often needed. Many paintings were therefore varnished several times over the centuries, sometimes with tinted varnishes that deliberately gave them a warm, golden tone, which nineteenth-century collectors associated with the work of the old masters. Distinguishing between these later layers and anything the artist applied is one of the conservator's hardest tasks.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first great public controversy erupted at the National Gallery in London after the Second World War. During the war the collection had been stored in a slate quarry in north Wales, and when the paintings returned, the gallery took the opportunity to clean a number of major works. An exhibition of cleaned pictures in 1947 drew enormous crowds, but it also attracted fierce criticism. Some art historians, the Austrian-born scholar Ernst Gombrich among them, argued that the old masters may have applied thin, tinted glazes over their paintings to soften and unify the colours, and that cleaning risked removing these along with the discoloured varnish. The dispute continued in academic journals for more than fifteen years. The gallery's conservators replied that they had found no technical evidence for such glazes in the works concerned.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Since then, science has transformed the conservator's work. Tiny samples taken from the edges of damaged areas, no bigger than a pinhead, can be mounted and examined under the microscope to reveal the sequence of layers from the canvas upwards. Infrared and ultraviolet imaging, which do not touch the painting at all, show where later paint has been added, and chemical analysis can identify the materials in each layer. Dr Paula Henriksen, a conservation scientist in Copenhagen, says that it is now usually possible to tell whether a layer is original before it is removed, although she admits that thin glazes which have partly soaked into the paint beneath can still be extremely hard to detect.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most famous restoration of recent times was that of Michelangelo's frescoes in the Sistine Chapel in Rome, a project carried out between 1980 and 1994. Centuries of candle smoke, dust and layers of animal glue applied by earlier restorers had given the ceiling a dark, sombre appearance, and many scholars had built their understanding of Michelangelo around it, describing him as a painter who was indifferent to colour. When the cleaning revealed bright pinks, greens and oranges, some critics claimed that the restorers had removed a final layer of shading added by the artist himself. Most specialists now accept that the bright colours are original, but the episode showed how strongly expectations can shape what people believe a painting should look like.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Faced with such uncertainty, many conservators have adopted a cautious approach, preferring to do too little rather than too much. Rather than removing all the varnish, they reduce it, leaving a thin layer that protects the paint and evens out the surface. This practice, sometimes called partial cleaning, has long been standard in a number of Italian and French museums, whereas British and American institutions have historically favoured more complete removal. Dr Marco Ferri of the University of Florence argues that partial cleaning respects the history of the object, since the painting that has come down to us is not the same as the one that left the artist's studio, and can never be made so.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is also a growing emphasis on reversibility, a principle now written into the professional codes of most conservation organisations. Modern synthetic varnishes are designed to remain stable for long periods and to be removable with mild solvents, so that any future conservator can undo today's work without harming the paint. Henriksen believes that this is perhaps the most important change of all. Earlier restorers often saw themselves as completing or improving a painting, whereas their modern successors regard themselves as caretakers whose decisions should, as far as possible, leave options open for those who come after them.
